title: The ages
hook: the Granth uses the four ages as a poetic frame for moral decline and renewal

segments.voice: Yesterday, vismaad: worlds below worlds, and wonder that grows as you learn. Your line was wonder keeps learning. Who did you tell your fact to? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

Things were better once. People say it about manners, music, neighbors, prices. The old Indian world gave that feeling a grand shape: the ages, each one darker than the one before, sliding toward the last and hardest, the Kaljug. The Gurus inherited that frame. They didn't throw it away. But in their hands it stops being a calendar to calculate and becomes something closer to a mirror. Today's word is the Granth's word for an age, and the chariot Guru Nanak gives each one.
screen: `THINGS WERE BETTER ONCE.` → `THE AGES, DARKER AND DARKER.` → `NOT A CALENDAR. A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Jug, or yuga, means an age. The Granth names them: Satjug, Treta, Duapar, and Kaljug, the dark age, the one the hymns place us in. Second, the chariots. In a salok in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives each age a chariot and a driver. In paraphrase: in Satjug, contentment was the chariot and righteousness the charioteer; in Treta, restraint was the chariot and strength the charioteer; in Duapar, austerity was the chariot and truth the charioteer; in Kaljug, the fire of craving is the chariot and falsehood holds the reins. Notice what changes. Not the scenery. The virtues. Each age is described by what's driving people. Third, the mirror. That's why it reads as poetry about the heart, not a timetable. The Kaljug isn't only out there in history. It's wherever craving is the vehicle and a lie is steering. And Satjug, in that same picture, is wherever contentment carries a life and righteousness guides it. A single day can pass through more than one age. Fourth, renewal. The Granth doesn't leave the dark age hopeless. The very first salok of the Japji says the True One was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true. The ages turn; the True One doesn't. And the hymns point to the Name, and to singing the praise, as what carries a person through a dark age. Decline is real. So is the way back.
screen: `JUG: AN AGE.` · `A CHARIOT AND A DRIVER FOR EACH AGE.` · `THE AGES AS A MIRROR OF THE HEART.` · `TRUE THROUGH THE AGES.` · then, large: `AGES TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice decline and renewal. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or so. Where was craving the chariot, and something false at the reins: a rush, a grab, a small lie to get by? Just notice it, without scolding. Now look for the other kind of moment: when contentment carried you and something true was steering. A meal enjoyed, an honest word. Breathe in the first, breathe out the second. Both ages pass through one life. The bell holds the time.
Jug. An age; the Granth uses the ages, from Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for decline and renewal, with a chariot and a driver for each. Today's word.
Your line: ages turn. Today, when you catch craving at the reins, swap the driver: one honest choice, one moment of enough. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the Granth's ages, Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for the state of the heart, and hold that the Name and singing God's praise carry a person through the dark age.

notes: Please confirm Ang 470 for the chariot salok and each age's chariot and charioteer as paraphrased (Satjug: contentment and dharam; Treta: restraint/jat and strength; Duapar: tapa and truth; Kaljug: the fire of craving and falsehood).
Please confirm that the Japji's opening salok ('aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach') is fairly paraphrased.
'The hymns point to the Name, and to singing the praise, as what carries a person through a dark age' is general; a specific Ang (e.g. 'kaljug meh kirtan pardhana') could be added after checking.
'Jug is the Punjabi form of yuga' is the one word-origin claim; please confirm.
